paper.title: HYDRA: A Multi-Level Hierarchy-Driven Approach for Robust Anomaly Detection in Time Series
paper.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data (PACMMOD), vol. 4, no. 3, article 197, pp. 1-30
paper.abstract: Time-series anomaly detection is critical across various domains. Despite advances in neural networks and foundation models, recent studies show that traditional data mining methods remain highly competitive due to their effectiveness and scalability. However, these approaches suffer from distinct limitations: discord-based methods fail in the presence of repeated anomalies, whereas clustering-based techniques, though mitigating this issue, struggle to capture fine-grained deviations. Moreover, both approaches rely on distance computation, whose effectiveness fundamentally depends on data normalization, with z-score serving as the de facto standard. However, we observe that while normalization reduces scale bias and can enhance anomaly detectability, it may also suppress amplitude-driven anomalies, making the choice of an appropriate normalization scheme both critical and non-trivial. To address these challenges, we propose HYDRA, a multi-level hierarchical and unsupervised approach that integrates the strengths of distance-based methods while reducing reliance on explicit normalization. HYDRA (i) employs a lightweight approximate nearest-neighbor detector with graph-based selection to identify representative subsequences; (ii) constructs multi-resolution representations of the time series and aggregates anomaly evidence from fine to coarse scales; and (iii) introduces a hierarchical ensemble mechanism that fuses level-wise scores to improve robustness against contamination and scale imbalance. This design allows HYDRA to detect diverse anomaly types, from short, isolated discords to long, persistent deviations, allowing it to detect patterns overlooked by single-scale methods. Extensive evaluation on 40 univariate and multivariate time-series anomaly detection datasets from the TSB-AD benchmark demonstrates that HYDRA achieves state-of-the-art performance, ranking first among 40 competing algorithms, while maintaining scalability to ultra-long sequences.

compatibility.reason: HYDRA is an unsupervised, training-free subsequence-based anomaly detector: it scores every sliding window by hierarchical nearest-neighbor compression and fuses level-wise scores into a point-wise anomaly score, evaluated on the TSB-AD benchmark (AUROC/AUPRC-style metrics via TSB_AD.evaluation.metrics.get_metrics). Both univariate and multivariate inputs are supported: HYDRA_approx.compress_and_score_multi accepts a 1-D array (reshaped to a single channel) or a 2-D array (each channel z-scored column-wise before windowing), and HYDRA/main.py branches on data.shape[1] == 1 for window selection. Because there is no learned/trainable parameter set, the only applicable training schema is 'naive' (fit-free scoring of the test series); there is no pretrained checkpoint so zero-shot / zero-shot-cross-dataset schemas do not apply, and no joint multi-dataset 'all_in_one' training exists in the official code.
compatibility.compute_device_evidence: The enabled algorithm (mode='approx', used by HYDRA/main.py::run_HYDRA) is implemented in HYDRA/models/HYDRA_approx.py and HYDRA/models/HNSW_index.py using only numpy, hnswlib (optional) or sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors — no torch tensors or .cuda() calls anywhere in the model path. HYDRA/models/HYDRA_exact.py likewise uses only numpy/sklearn. HYDRA/main.py imports torch solely to seed RNGs (torch.manual_seed / torch.cuda.manual_seed / torch.cuda.manual_seed_all) and prints torch.cuda.is_available(); these calls are no-ops on a CPU-only machine and no computation is dispatched to the GPU, so the reproduction runs on CPU. Uncertainty: hnswlib is listed in requirements.txt but is optional (HNSW_index.py falls back to sklearn), so a CPU-only install is sufficient.
compatibility.interface_notes: Official output is a 1-D point-wise anomaly score array aligned to the input series: ensemble_maxpool_windows returns ts_score_final produced by reverse_windowing_min, which maps window scores back to length-T timepoint scores (averaging over overlapping windows). Higher score = more anomalous. HYDRA/main.py additionally MinMax-scales the score to [0,1] and derives a binary prediction via mean+3*std threshold, but only the continuous score is needed by EasyTSAD.
